t.2.106.1: Riding in a chariot whose rumble was deep and resonant, the lord Bharata, of great renown, swiftly entered Ayodhyā.
t.2.106.2: He beheld the city haunted by cats and owls, its men and elephants hidden away, like a black and lightless night overwhelmed by darkness.
t.2.106.3: She was alone and afflicted, like Rohiṇī, the beloved wife of Rāhu's foe, whose radiance blazes with splendour, when she is oppressed by a planet that has risen against her.
t.2.106.4: She was like a shrunken mountain river, its scanty water warm and stirred up, its birds scorched by the heat, its fish, jhaṣas and crocodiles lying hidden.
t.2.106.5: It was like a smokeless, gold-hued flame risen from the sacrificial fire which, after being sprinkled with the oblation, has gone out.
t.2.106.6: It was like an army fallen into ruin in a great battle, its armor shattered, its elephants, horses, chariots and banners broken, and its foremost heroes slain.
t.2.106.7: He saw the city, which had once been foaming and roaring, now silent, like a wave of the ocean that had surged up, tossed by the wind, and fallen soundless once the wind had died away.
t.2.106.8: It was like a sacrificial altar forsaken by all its sacrificial implements and by its comely priests, its clamor gone silent once the time of the soma-pressing had passed.
t.2.106.9: She was like the chief cow of the herd, abandoned by the bull, standing distressed in the middle of the cowpen, not grazing on the fresh grass, and pining with longing.
t.2.106.10: It was like a new string of pearls stripped of its excellent, high-born gems, gems dazzling with radiance, deeply lustrous, as though ablaze.
t.2.106.11: It seemed like the earth suddenly shaken from its place, fallen low through the exhaustion of its merit, like a star dropped from heaven with the spread of its radiance withdrawn.
t.2.106.12: She was like a forest creeper that, at the end of spring, had been laden with flowers and graced by intoxicated bees, but was now scorched by a swiftly spreading forest fire and withered.
t.2.106.13: The whole city, its merchants dazed and its stalls and shops closed up, was like the sky covered with clouds, its moon and stars hidden from view.
t.2.106.14: It was like an uncleaned drinking-ground in the open air whose revelers have been struck down, strewn all over with broken cups whose choice liquor is spent.
t.2.106.15: It was like a ruined, collapsed watering-shed, its floor broken up and sunken, strewn with shattered vessels, its water all used up.
t.2.106.16: She was like the bowstring of mighty warriors, long and drawn taut, its loops fastened, yet cut through by arrows and fallen from the bow onto the ground.
t.2.106.17: It was like a feeble young mare, ridden hard and suddenly by a battle-loving horseman, then stripped of her harness and turned loose.
t.2.106.18: It was like the radiance of the sun when the rainy season has set in deep, the sun having entered a mass of clouds, its light veiled by dark rain-clouds.
t.2.106.19: But the illustrious Bharata, son of Daśaratha, being seated in his chariot, spoke these words to the charioteer who was driving the finest of chariots.
t.2.106.20: Why is it, then, that today the deep, swelling sound of song and music is not heard in Ayodhyā as it was before?
t.2.106.21: The heady scents of vāruṇī wine, the pervading fragrance of garlands, and the scent of burning agaru incense no longer waft on every side.
t.2.106.22: The rumble of the finest carriages, the deep, rich neighing of horses, the trumpeting of rutting elephants and the mighty clatter of chariots are no longer heard in this city now that Rāma has been banished.
t.2.106.23: The great highways of Ayodhyā no longer shine with young men in handsome attire, walking with heads held high as they throng along them.
t.2.106.24: Lamenting thus in many ways, he entered his father's dwelling, bereft of that lord of men, like a cave bereft of its lion.
